title: Janusz Korczak
hookLine: a doctor and teacher who went with his orphans to Treblinka

cards: An orphanage where the children run a court. Any child can bring a complaint, even against a teacher, even against the director. The judges are children too.
The house has its own newspaper and its own parliament, and a belief that a child's sorrow is never small just because the child is.
The director is a doctor with a gray beard, who also writes stories for children and talks to them on the radio. He thinks children are already people, not people-in-waiting.

teach.h: A PEN NAME, A DOCTOR, AN ORPHANAGE.
teach.b: Janusz Korczak was a pen name. He was born Henryk Goldszmit, a Polish Jew, and became a pediatrician, a writer of children's books, and the director of an orphanage for Jewish children in Warsaw.
His whole life argued one thing: that children deserve respect now, not later.

teach.h: BEGGING FOR FOOD IN THE GHETTO.
teach.b: When the ghetto was sealed, the orphanage was forced inside the walls, and Korczak went with it. He went out each day to beg for food, for medicine, for coal, for anything that would keep his children alive.
At night he kept a diary, which survived. Then the deportations came. The story, as witnesses remembered it, is that when the Germans came for the orphans, Korczak would not leave them.
He and his staff, among them his colleague Stefania Wilczynska, walked with the children through the streets to the trains, in rows, some say carrying a flag.
The story is also told that he was offered a way to save himself, and refused. They were taken to Treblinka, and none of them came back.

The psalm calls God by a tender name: "A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows." That is how God is described: the one who stands beside those who have no one. Korczak is not remembered for working wonders.
He was a tired doctor with a diary and a house full of children.

teach.h: HE WOULD NOT LET THEM GO ALONE.
teach.b: But at the end, when he could not protect them, he would not let them go alone.
The orphans were his. He stayed with them.

how: Korczak's story is read in Jewish schools and at Holocaust memorial gatherings, and his ideas about respecting children are still taught to teachers and caregivers.

practice: Bring to mind someone who depends on others right now: a child, a parent growing frail, a friend who is sick, a neighbor living alone.
Let their face come clearly, and let one small way of being with them take shape: a visit, a call, sitting beside them, listening to the end of a long story.

wordCard.voice: Janusz Korczak. The doctor and teacher who ran a Warsaw orphanage like a children's republic, and who walked with his orphans to the trains. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: he stayed with them. Children deserve respect now, not later, and he lived it to the end. Rest well.
